extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of political economy; policymakers and reformers interested in population, poverty, and social theory
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century political-economy critique that assesses the Malthusian claim that population growth necessarily presses upon subsistence and produces poverty; argues by examining analogies, empirical cases, and logical structure. Intended as an argument against the theory and a proposal to test it by facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish social causes from natural limits
rubrics_metrics.description: “I assert that the injustice of society, not the niggardliness of nature, is the cause of the want and misery which the current theory attributes to over-population.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of poverty by examining social arrangements (absentee landlords, extraction of at least a fourth of net produce, resident landlords with their household and agents, state church, police and army) that divert produce and undermine producers' hope, thrift and energy. Anti-pattern: attributing misery directly to 'natural laws' without inspecting institutional extraction and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of analogy from animal/vegetable reproduction to humans
rubrics_metrics.description: The analogy that because animals and plants multiply rapidly they press against subsistence and thus humans must do likewise is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge analogical arguments by whether the compared cases share the critical causal structures: animals/plants cannot expand their food-supply but humans can (e.g., raising salmon spawn, agriculture, removing predators). Examples: pair of salmon or rabbits vs human capacity to extend food production. Anti-pattern: treating superficial numeric similarity of reproductive power as proof of identical dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether humans can increase subsistence (human agency alters limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is unique in that the increase of men can involve an increase of his food ("the increase of men that has brought about the increase of food").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate population effects by considering technological, organizational, and ecological changes humans create (roads, farming methods, domestication, removal of predators) that can raise per-capita subsistence. Use historical examples (United States growth producing more food per capita) to test the claim that more people necessarily reduce subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs global limits of subsistence
rubrics_metrics.description: The limit of subsistence in any particular place is not the physical limit of that place, but the physical limit of the globe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing pressures of population in a locality, consider trade, migration of resources, and the ability to draw subsistence from wider areas (example: London drawing upon the whole globe). Do not assume local land area alone fixes subsistence limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'diminishing productiveness' as relative, not absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of diminishing productiveness holds relatively; taken absolutely (on a global scale) it is false because matter and force are indestructible and human agency redistributes productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique claims that more labor will always yield proportionally less by examining whether declines in a particular land’s yield reflect shifting returns among lands or general, absolute limits. Consider technological and organizational advances that alter productive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for evolving human wants and their effect on population dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is the only animal whose desires increase as they are fed; as comfort and intellectual life rise, birth rates tend to decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate population projections by including sociocultural factors: increase in quality-of-life and intellectual development typically reduces birth rates (examples: fewer births among affluent/educated classes; higher proportion of births in frontier or impoverished populations). Avoid assuming a fixed reproductive instinct unaffected by social development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test theories by facts about wealth-producing power, not by abstract claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The real question is whether increase of population tends to reduce the amount of wealth that can be produced by a given amount of labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess population theories empirically: measure whether per-unit-labor wealth-producing power falls with population growth, using historical and comparative data rather than relying on metaphorical or purely deductive analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure productive power by total expenditure of productive effort (not just staples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of any population to produce the necessaries of life is not to be measured by the necessaries actually produced, but by the expenditure of power in all modes ("a set of diamonds has a value equal to so many barrels of flour").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating changes in productive capacity, account for how labor and resources are allocated across uses (luxury vs subsistence, military, ceremonial). Avoid narrow metrics that ignore non-food wealth or non-productive consumption that still reflect productive capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical criterion: richer where population is denser
rubrics_metrics.description: On the same level of civilization and stage of productive arts, the most populous countries are always the most wealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-sectional and historical comparisons (e.g., England vs Brazil, Eastern vs Western U.S., California development) to test whether denser populations correlate with greater wealth per capita and higher total production efficiency. Beware confounders (stage of technology, institutions) and interpret direction of causation carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret instances of falling wages in growing populations through distribution and institutional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases where wages fall despite increased population (example: California) often reflect inequality of distribution and social/institutional factors rather than diminished productive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyzing apparent counterexamples to the claim that population increases wealth, investigate improvements in infrastructure and efficiency (roads, railroads, telegraphs, machinery), shifts in consumption (more non-producers supported), and distributional changes that concentrate gains. Avoid assuming falling wages imply nature's 'niggardliness' without checking distributional context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical rigor: beware undistributed middle and unwarranted premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasoning supporting the doctrine often rests on an unwarranted assumption, 'an undistributed middle', making the argument logically invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arguments for hidden premises or invalid inference patterns. Demand that analogies and syllogisms distribute middle terms correctly and that premises are empirically grounded rather than assumed.
